title: Antiepileptic Drugs
summary: Mechanisms of seizure drugs and how they are chosen.

lessons.title: Seizure Mechanisms

levels.kid:
Your brain cells talk with tiny electric sparks. Normally they take turns, like kids in a class raising hands one at a time.

A **seizure** is when lots of brain cells start firing at the same time, all together, like the whole class shouting at once. The brain can't do its normal jobs for a little while. A person might shake, stare, or fall.

The brain has a **gas pedal** (signals that excite cells) and **brakes** (signals that calm cells). A seizure happens when the gas is too strong or the brakes are too weak.

Seizure medicines work by easing off the gas or pressing harder on the brakes, so the brain cells go back to taking turns.
levels.hs:
A **seizure** is a burst of abnormal, excessive and **synchronized** electrical activity in the brain. **Epilepsy** is a tendency to have repeated, unprovoked seizures.

**Excitation vs inhibition.** Neurons balance excitatory signals (mainly **glutamate**) with inhibitory signals (mainly **GABA**). Seizures arise when this balance tips toward excitation.

**What drives firing:**
- **Sodium channels** open to start an action potential.
- **Calcium channels** trigger transmitter release, and **T-type calcium channels** in the thalamus help create rhythmic firing.
- **GABA-A receptors** let chloride in to calm neurons.

**Types of seizures:**
- **Focal** seizures start in one area of one hemisphere. Symptoms depend on that area, for example twitching of one hand if the motor cortex is involved.
- **Generalized** seizures involve both hemispheres from the start. Examples are **tonic-clonic** (stiffening then jerking), **absence** (brief staring spells, common in children) and **myoclonic** (quick jerks).

**Why this matters for drugs:** each seizure drug targets part of the machinery: blocking sodium or calcium channels, boosting GABA, or reducing glutamate. Matching the drug to the seizure type matters, because some drugs that help focal seizures can make absence or myoclonic seizures worse.
levels.college:
**Definitions.** A seizure is a transient occurrence of signs or symptoms due to abnormal excessive or synchronous neuronal activity. Epilepsy (ILAE practical definition) is diagnosed after two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart, one unprovoked seizure with a high recurrence risk, or an epilepsy syndrome.

**Cellular events.** The hallmark of an interictal spike is the **paroxysmal depolarization shift (PDS)**: a large, prolonged depolarization driven by AMPA/NMDA glutamate currents and voltage-gated Ca2+ entry, firing a burst of sodium action potentials, followed by GABA- and K+-mediated hyperpolarization. Seizures emerge when this surround inhibition fails and bursting recruits neighboring cortex.

**Focal onset and spread.** Spread occurs through local recurrent excitatory circuits, loss of inhibition and propagation through corticocortical and thalamocortical pathways. High-frequency firing depends on rapid recovery of Na+ channels from inactivation, which is why use-dependent Na+ channel blockers suppress it.

**Absence seizures** reflect a different circuit: oscillations between the cortex, thalamic relay neurons and the GABAergic **reticular thalamic nucleus**. Hyperpolarization de-inactivates **T-type (Cav3) Ca2+ channels**, producing low-threshold spikes and the classic **3 Hz spike-and-wave** EEG. GABA-B activation deepens hyperpolarization, so some GABA-enhancing drugs (tiagabine, vigabatrin) can worsen absences.

**Mechanistic drug classes:**
- Na+ channel blockade: phenytoin, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, lacosamide.
- T-type Ca2+ blockade: ethosuximide.
- GABA enhancement: benzodiazepines, phenobarbital, vigabatrin, tiagabine.
- Synaptic release modulation: levetiracetam (SV2A), gabapentinoids (α2δ).
- Glutamate antagonism: perampanel (AMPA).

**Etiologies** include genetic, structural (stroke, tumor, cortical dysplasia, hippocampal sclerosis), metabolic (hyponatremia, hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia), infectious, immune and unknown. Provoked seizures are treated by correcting the cause, not with long-term antiseizure drugs.
levels.phd:
**Ictogenesis versus epileptogenesis.** Ictogenesis is the transition from interictal to ictal activity; epileptogenesis is the slow process by which a normal brain becomes epileptic after an insult. Every currently approved antiseizure medication (ASM) is antiictogenic: none has convincingly been shown to prevent epilepsy in humans, which is why the field now prefers "antiseizure" to "antiepileptic". Candidate antiepileptogenic targets include mTOR (rapamycin analogues in tuberous sclerosis models), neuroinflammation (IL-1β, HMGB1–TLR4), TGF-β signaling after blood–brain barrier leakage of albumin, and REST-mediated transcriptional changes.

**Network mechanisms.** Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy shows hippocampal sclerosis with loss of CA1/CA3 and hilar interneurons, **mossy fiber sprouting** forming recurrent excitatory loops onto dentate granule cells, and dispersion of granule cells. Ictal onset patterns differ: low-voltage fast activity often reflects interneuron-driven synchronization, while hypersynchronous onsets reflect principal-cell recruitment. Paradoxically, intense interneuron firing can initiate seizures by producing large GABA-A-mediated chloride loads, depolarizing EGABA and causing extracellular K+ accumulation.

**Chloride homeostasis.** NKCC1 (Cl− in) dominates in immature neurons and KCC2 (Cl− out) in mature ones. After injury or in neonatal brain, low KCC2 makes GABA depolarizing, weakening benzodiazepine and phenobarbital efficacy; bumetanide was tested as an NKCC1 blocker in neonatal seizures but failed in trials (NEMO).

**Channelopathies teach pharmacology.** SCN1A loss-of-function (Dravet syndrome) impairs Nav1.1 in inhibitory interneurons, so further Na+ channel blockade worsens seizures. SCN2A and SCN8A gain-of-function variants, in contrast, may respond well to Na+ blockers. KCNQ2 (M-current) variants cause neonatal epilepsy; GABRG2 and CACNA1H variants link to absence phenotypes. Precision approaches (gene-specific ASM choice, antisense oligonucleotides upregulating SCN1A expression) are emerging.

**Drug resistance** (failure of two appropriately chosen, tolerated ASMs) affects roughly a third of patients. Hypotheses include target alteration, efflux transporter overexpression at the BBB (P-glycoprotein), network rewiring and intrinsic severity.
levels.expert:
**Classify before you prescribe.** The first question is not "which drug" but "is this a seizure, is it provoked, and what type". Syncope with brief myoclonic jerks, psychogenic nonepileptic events and convulsive syncope are frequent mimics. Check glucose, sodium, calcium and magnesium, toxicology, sleep deprivation and alcohol withdrawal before labelling epilepsy. A provoked seizure from hyponatremia needs sodium correction, not lifelong medication.

**Type drives drug choice.** Focal epilepsy: lamotrigine and levetiracetam are common first choices, with carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine and lacosamide as alternatives. Generalized epilepsy (juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, generalized tonic-clonic): valproate is most effective but restricted in people who could become pregnant, so levetiracetam or lamotrigine are often used. Absence epilepsy in children: ethosuximide is first-line (better tolerated than valproate with similar efficacy, superior to lamotrigine in the Childhood Absence Epilepsy trial).

**The classic pitfall** is carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine or phenytoin given for unrecognized generalized epilepsy: absences and myoclonus can worsen, and in Dravet syndrome Na+ channel blockers can precipitate status. If a teenager with "focal" seizures has morning jerks and photosensitivity, rethink juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.

**EEG and imaging.** A routine EEG is normal in many people with epilepsy; sleep-deprived and prolonged recordings increase yield. MRI with an epilepsy protocol looks for hippocampal sclerosis, cortical dysplasia and tumors.

**Drug resistance changes the plan.** After two failed appropriate ASMs, the chance of seizure freedom with each additional drug is small. Refer to an epilepsy center for video-EEG monitoring and surgical evaluation: anterior temporal lobectomy for mesial temporal lobe epilepsy produces seizure freedom far more often than continued medical therapy (Wiebe et al., 2001). Laser interstitial thermal therapy, responsive neurostimulation, vagus nerve stimulation and deep brain stimulation of the anterior thalamus are further options, the bridge between pharmacology and neurosurgery.

keyPoints: A seizure is excessive, synchronized neuronal firing; epilepsy is a tendency to recurrent unprovoked seizures.
Seizures reflect excitation (glutamate, Na+/Ca2+ channels) overpowering inhibition (GABA).
Absence seizures arise from thalamocortical T-type Ca2+ oscillations (3 Hz spike-and-wave).
Na+ channel blockers can worsen absence, myoclonic seizures and Dravet syndrome (SCN1A).
Current drugs are antiseizure, not antiepileptogenic; about a third of patients are drug-resistant.
Two failed appropriate drugs = drug-resistant epilepsy: refer for surgical evaluation.

lessons.title: Sodium Channel Blockers

levels.kid:
To send a message, a brain cell opens tiny doors called **sodium channels**. Sodium rushes in and the cell fires.

After each fire, the door needs a short rest before it can open again. In a seizure, cells fire super fast, over and over.

**Sodium channel blocker** medicines sit on the doors while they rest. That makes the rest a bit longer. Normal, slow messages still get through, but super fast seizure firing gets slowed down.

It's like a gate that lets people walk through normally but stops a stampede.

These medicines can have side effects, so doctors check carefully which one fits each person.
levels.hs:
**Voltage-gated sodium channels** open to start each action potential. After opening they flip into an **inactivated** state and must recover before opening again.

**How the drugs work:** sodium channel blockers bind mostly to the **inactivated** channel and slow its recovery. Neurons firing rapidly, as in a seizure, have many inactivated channels, so they are blocked the most. This is called **use-dependent block**: normal brain activity is mostly spared.

**Key drugs:**
- **Phenytoin**: an old drug for focal and tonic-clonic seizures. Side effects include gum overgrowth, extra body hair, unsteady walking and jerky eye movements (nystagmus). Its blood level can climb sharply with small changes because the liver enzymes that break it down get saturated.
- **Carbamazepine**: used for focal seizures and trigeminal neuralgia (facial nerve pain). It can lower blood sodium and, rarely, cause serious skin reactions or low blood counts.
- **Oxcarbazepine**: a relative of carbamazepine with fewer drug interactions but more low-sodium problems.
- **Lamotrigine**: well tolerated and safer in pregnancy, but must be started slowly because of a rare, dangerous rash.
- **Lacosamide**: works on a slower form of inactivation.

These drugs can make absence and myoclonic seizures worse, so diagnosis comes first.
levels.college:
**Mechanism.** Nav channels cycle through resting, open and inactivated states. Phenytoin, carbamazepine and lamotrigine bind with higher affinity to the **fast-inactivated** state (a modulated-receptor model), stabilizing it and slowing recovery. Block accumulates during high-frequency firing (**use- and frequency-dependence**), so sustained repetitive firing is suppressed while single action potentials pass. **Lacosamide** instead enhances **slow inactivation**, a distinct conformational state reached over seconds.

**Phenytoin**
- **Zero-order (Michaelis–Menten) kinetics** at therapeutic concentrations: CYP2C9/2C19 saturate, so small dose increases cause disproportionate rises in level.
- Highly albumin-bound: in hypoalbuminemia or uremia the free fraction rises, so total levels mislead.
- Toxicity: nystagmus, ataxia, diplopia, sedation. Chronic: gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, coarse facies, osteomalacia (vitamin D catabolism), megaloblastic anemia (folate), peripheral neuropathy.
- Teratogen (fetal hydantoin syndrome). Strong CYP inducer.
- IV phenytoin causes hypotension and arrhythmias if infused fast and tissue injury (purple glove syndrome); **fosphenytoin** is a water-soluble prodrug that reduces these problems.

**Carbamazepine**
- Strong CYP3A4 inducer and **autoinducer** (its own half-life shortens over weeks).
- SIADH-like hyponatremia, agranulocytosis/aplastic anemia, hepatotoxicity, teratogenicity (neural tube defects).
- **HLA-B*15:02** (common in people of Southeast Asian ancestry) strongly predicts SJS/TEN; screen before starting. HLA-A*31:01 is linked to DRESS and other reactions.

**Oxcarbazepine/eslicarbazepine:** keto analogues avoiding the epoxide metabolite, weaker induction, more hyponatremia.

**Lamotrigine:** also inhibits glutamate release; slow titration reduces rash risk. **Valproate inhibits its glucuronidation** (raises levels, higher rash risk); estrogen-containing contraceptives and pregnancy induce glucuronidation (lower levels).

**Lacosamide:** few interactions; PR interval prolongation.
levels.phd:
**Structural pharmacology.** Cryo-EM of human Nav1.7 and Nav1.5 with local anesthetic-like drugs places the classical anticonvulsant site in the central cavity below the selectivity filter, lined by S6 residues of domains III and IV (Nav1.2 equivalents of the Ragsdale F1764/Y1771 residues). Fast inactivation by the IFM motif reshapes the fenestrations and cavity, explaining state-dependent affinity. Phenytoin, carbamazepine and lamotrigine share an overlapping site but differ in binding kinetics: carbamazepine binds and unbinds quickly, phenytoin more slowly, which may matter for blocking long depolarizations versus brief bursts.

**Persistent and resurgent currents.** A small non-inactivating persistent Na+ current (INaP) amplifies subthreshold depolarizations and supports bursting; resurgent current facilitates high-frequency firing. Cenobamate and, to a degree, lacosamide preferentially reduce INaP, and newer Nav1.6-selective inhibitors (in trials for SCN8A encephalopathy) aim to spare Nav1.1 in interneurons.

**Genotype–drug matching.** SCN1A loss-of-function in Dravet syndrome reduces interneuron excitability, so nonselective blockade worsens disinhibition. Conversely, SCN2A gain-of-function variants with early-onset epilepsy (often within the first months of life) and SCN8A gain-of-function variants often respond to high-level Na+ blockade, while later-onset SCN2A loss-of-function phenotypes do not.

**Pharmacogenomics.** HLA-B*15:02 presents carbamazepine directly to T-cell receptors in a non-classical, non-covalent manner (the pharmacological interaction, p-i, concept), producing cytotoxic CD8+ responses with granulysin-mediated keratinocyte death. The association is ancestry-specific; it also extends to phenytoin, oxcarbazepine and probably lamotrigine to lesser degrees. CYP2C9*3 carriers clear phenytoin slowly and have higher toxicity and SJS risk; CPIC guidance integrates both HLA-B*15:02 and CYP2C9.

**Kinetic oddities.** Phenytoin's saturable clearance means the time to reach steady state lengthens as concentration rises; carbamazepine's autoinduction completes over a few weeks. Both are examples of why therapeutic drug monitoring remains central for older ASMs.
levels.expert:
**Choosing among them.** For newly diagnosed focal epilepsy, the SANAD II trial found lamotrigine better than levetiracetam and zonisamide on time to treatment failure, supporting lamotrigine as a first choice when slow titration is acceptable. Carbamazepine remains effective but its interactions and induction (lowering levels of hormonal contraceptives, warfarin, many antiretrovirals and chemotherapies) make it less attractive in complex patients.

**Practical pitfalls:**
- **Phenytoin levels:** correct for albumin or measure free level in ICU, elderly, renal failure and pregnancy. A small change can push a patient from therapeutic into ataxic toxicity because of saturable kinetics.
- **IV phenytoin:** infuse slowly with cardiac monitoring (hypotension, bradyarrhythmia); prefer fosphenytoin when available.
- **Carbamazepine:** check HLA-B*15:02 in at-risk ancestry before starting; check sodium and blood counts; warn about rash and fever in the first months.
- **Oxcarbazepine:** hyponatremia is common, especially in older patients and with diuretics.
- **Lamotrigine:** never restart at the previous level after missing several days; re-titrate. Adding valproate requires slower titration; starting or stopping an estrogen pill changes levels. Rash with fever, mucosal involvement or eosinophilia means stop immediately.
- **Lacosamide:** baseline ECG in conduction disease; avoid combining with other PR-prolonging drugs when possible.

**Pregnancy.** Lamotrigine and levetiracetam have among the lowest malformation rates in pregnancy registries; phenytoin and carbamazepine are intermediate. Lamotrigine clearance rises sharply in pregnancy, so levels are monitored and adjusted, then reduced after delivery.

**Diagnostic mismatch.** If seizures increase after starting a Na+ blocker, consider a misdiagnosed generalized syndrome (juvenile myoclonic epilepsy) or an SCN1A-related epilepsy before simply increasing the drug.

keyPoints: Na+ channel blockers bind the inactivated channel: use-dependent block of rapid firing.
Phenytoin: zero-order kinetics, gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, nystagmus/ataxia, teratogen; fosphenytoin is the safer IV prodrug.
Carbamazepine: autoinduction, CYP3A4 induction, hyponatremia, agranulocytosis; HLA-B*15:02 predicts SJS/TEN.
Lamotrigine: slow titration for rash; valproate raises and estrogen lowers its levels.
Lacosamide enhances slow inactivation and can prolong the PR interval.
These drugs can worsen absence, myoclonic seizures and Dravet syndrome.

lessons.title: GABAergic and Calcium Channel Drugs

levels.kid:
Some seizure medicines work on the brain's **brakes**. The brain's main brake signal is called **GABA**. These medicines help GABA work better, or keep more GABA around, so brain cells stay calm.

Other seizure medicines work on **calcium doors**. Calcium helps brain cells pass messages and, in one part of the brain, helps make a fast on-off rhythm.

One kind of seizure, called an **absence seizure**, makes kids stare blankly for a few seconds. A medicine called **ethosuximide** blocks special calcium doors deep in the brain and stops that rhythm.

So: some medicines press the brakes, and some close calcium doors.
levels.hs:
**Drugs that boost GABA** (the main inhibitory transmitter):
- **Benzodiazepines** (lorazepam, diazepam, midazolam, clobazam) make GABA-A receptors open more often. They are excellent for stopping seizures fast, but tolerance and sleepiness limit long-term use.
- **Phenobarbital** (a barbiturate) keeps GABA-A channels open longer. It is cheap and still widely used worldwide and in newborns, but it is very sedating.
- **Vigabatrin** permanently blocks the enzyme that breaks down GABA (GABA transaminase), so GABA builds up. It is used for **infantile spasms**, especially in tuberous sclerosis. It can cause permanent loss of side vision, so eyes are checked.
- **Tiagabine** blocks the reuptake of GABA so it stays in the synapse longer.

**Drugs that act on calcium channels:**
- **Ethosuximide** blocks **T-type calcium channels** in the thalamus and is first-line for childhood **absence seizures**. It does not treat tonic-clonic seizures.
- **Gabapentin** and **pregabalin** bind a helper part of calcium channels called **α2δ**, reducing the release of excitatory transmitters. They are modest seizure drugs but are widely used for nerve pain. They are cleared by the kidneys and have few drug interactions.

Knowing which part of the brain's machinery each drug targets helps doctors pick the right one for each seizure type.
levels.college:
**GABA-A positive modulators**
- **Benzodiazepines** increase opening frequency at the α/γ2 interface. Rescue and status treatment; **clobazam** (a 1,5-benzodiazepine) is used as adjunct therapy, notably in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome. Tolerance to the anticonvulsant effect develops with chronic use; abrupt withdrawal can trigger seizures.
- **Phenobarbital** increases opening duration and directly gates at higher concentrations; also reduces AMPA/kainate responses. Long half-life, strong CYP inducer, sedation, cognitive and behavioral effects in children, connective tissue disorders. Still first-line for neonatal seizures in many guidelines. **Primidone** is metabolized to phenobarbital and PEMA (also used for essential tremor).

**GABA metabolism and transport**
- **Vigabatrin**: irreversible suicide inhibitor of **GABA transaminase (GABA-T)**; effect outlasts plasma half-life. First-line for **infantile spasms in tuberous sclerosis complex**; adjunct in refractory focal seizures. Risk of **irreversible bilateral concentric visual field constriction** (retinal toxicity), plus reversible MRI signal changes in infants.
- **Tiagabine**: selective **GAT-1** inhibitor. Adjunct for focal seizures; can provoke nonconvulsive status epilepticus, even in people without epilepsy.

**Calcium channel drugs**
- **Ethosuximide**: blocks **T-type (Cav3.1–3.3)** low-threshold currents in thalamic relay neurons. Narrow spectrum: absence only. Adverse effects: GI upset, fatigue, headache, rare blood dyscrasias and lupus-like reactions.
- **Gabapentin/pregabalin**: bind **α2δ-1** (and α2δ-2) auxiliary subunits, reducing trafficking of high-voltage-activated channels to presynaptic terminals and lowering release of glutamate, substance P and norepinephrine. Not GABA receptor agonists despite their names. Renally excreted unchanged; adjust in kidney disease. Gabapentin has saturable absorption via the L-amino acid transporter; pregabalin's is linear. Sedation, dizziness, peripheral edema; respiratory depression risk when combined with opioids. Can aggravate myoclonic seizures.

**Valproate and zonisamide** also reduce T-type current, contributing to their absence efficacy.
levels.phd:
**Benzodiazepine tolerance mechanisms.** Chronic exposure produces receptor uncoupling (reduced allosteric linkage between benzodiazepine and GABA sites), altered subunit composition (decreased α1, increased α4), receptor internalization and compensatory glutamatergic upregulation. Tolerance to the anticonvulsant effect limits chronic monotherapy; intermittent or rescue use preserves efficacy. Clobazam's lower sedative liability is attributed partly to its 1,5 structure and its active metabolite N-desmethylclobazam, which accumulates in CYP2C19 poor metabolizers.

**Vigabatrin pharmacology.** Vigabatrin is a GABA analogue that forms a covalent adduct with the pyridoxal phosphate cofactor of GABA-T. Brain GABA concentrations measured by magnetic resonance spectroscopy rise within hours and remain elevated for days, so the pharmacodynamic half-life is set by enzyme resynthesis. Retinal toxicity is linked to GABA accumulation and taurine deficiency in photoreceptors and amacrine cells in animal models; visual field loss is dose- and duration-related and generally irreversible. Only the S-enantiomer is active.

**T-type channels and thalamocortical rhythm.** In GAERS and WAG/Rij rat models, Cav3.1 knockout abolishes spike-wave discharges, and gain-of-function CACNA1H variants are associated with childhood absence epilepsy. Cortical initiation in the somatosensory cortex drives thalamic oscillations, recasting absence epilepsy as a corticothalamic network disorder rather than purely thalamic. Ethosuximide also reduces persistent Na+ and Ca2+-activated K+ currents at higher concentrations.

**α2δ biology.** α2δ-1 is upregulated in dorsal root ganglia after nerve injury, explaining gabapentinoid efficacy in neuropathic pain. α2δ-1 also binds thrombospondins to promote excitatory synaptogenesis; gabapentin blocks this interaction, suggesting synaptogenesis effects. The R217A α2δ-1 knock-in mouse, which cannot bind pregabalin, loses its analgesic action, confirming the target.

**Neonatal pharmacology.** Phenobarbital outperformed levetiracetam for neonatal seizures in the NEOLEV2 trial, consistent with GABA's remaining utility despite immature chloride gradients, although many seizures still persist and electrographic-only seizures are frequent.
levels.expert:
**Rescue therapy.** For a prolonged or clustered seizure at home, buccal or intranasal midazolam and rectal or intranasal diazepam are the standard benzodiazepine rescues. Families get a written seizure action plan specifying when to give rescue medicine and when to call emergency services.

**Clobazam** is a useful adjunct in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome and in many refractory epilepsies; watch sedation, drooling and behavior, and interactions with stiripentol and other CYP2C19 inhibitors (which raise N-desmethylclobazam).

**Phenobarbital** remains valuable worldwide because it is cheap and effective; in high-income settings, its cognitive effects, induction and withdrawal seizures on stopping push it lower. Tapering must be slow.

**Vigabatrin for infantile spasms.** In tuberous sclerosis complex, vigabatrin is first-line; for other etiologies, ACTH or oral steroids are often preferred or combined (the ICISS trial supported combining hormonal therapy with vigabatrin). Speed matters: delay in controlling hypsarrhythmia worsens developmental outcome. Arrange visual monitoring where possible, recognizing that infants cannot do formal perimetry, and reassess the need for continuing.

**Ethosuximide** is the best first choice for childhood absence epilepsy without generalized tonic-clonic seizures; if tonic-clonic seizures coexist, it will not cover them, so valproate (in boys or when appropriate) or lamotrigine are considered.

**Gabapentinoids in practice.** As antiseizure drugs they are weak and can aggravate myoclonus. Their major clinical role is neuropathic pain (postherpetic neuralgia, diabetic neuropathy). Adjust for kidney function, warn about dizziness, falls and edema, and be cautious combining them with opioids or other CNS depressants because of respiratory depression.

**Tiagabine** pitfall: new confusion or staring on tiagabine should prompt an EEG for nonconvulsive status.

keyPoints: Benzodiazepines (frequency) and phenobarbital (duration) enhance GABA-A; tolerance limits chronic benzodiazepine use.
Vigabatrin irreversibly inhibits GABA transaminase: first-line for infantile spasms in tuberous sclerosis; risk of permanent visual field loss.
Tiagabine blocks GAT-1 GABA reuptake and can provoke nonconvulsive status.
Ethosuximide blocks thalamic T-type Ca2+ channels: absence seizures only.
Gabapentin/pregabalin bind α2δ, reduce transmitter release, are renally cleared and mainly used for neuropathic pain.

lessons.title: Broad-Spectrum and Newer Agents

levels.kid:
Some seizure medicines are **broad-spectrum**. That means they work on many kinds of seizures, like a key that opens lots of locks.

**Valproate** is a strong one that works on many seizures. But it can be harmful to a baby growing inside a mom, so doctors are very careful with it.

**Levetiracetam** is used a lot because it is easy to take with other medicines. Some people feel grumpy on it.

**Topiramate** can make it harder to find words and can cause kidney stones.

Scientists keep inventing **newer medicines** for hard-to-treat seizures, including rare ones in children. Each one fixes a slightly different part of the brain's wiring.
levels.hs:
**Broad-spectrum** antiseizure drugs work against both focal and generalized seizures.

**Valproate** acts in several ways: it blocks sodium channels, blocks T-type calcium channels and raises GABA. It is very effective for generalized epilepsies such as juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. Problems: weight gain, tremor, hair thinning, rare liver failure (highest risk in very young children), pancreatitis and low platelets. It is the most harmful seizure drug in pregnancy, causing spinal cord defects (spina bifida), lower IQ and higher autism risk, so it is avoided in people who could become pregnant unless nothing else works.

**Levetiracetam** binds a protein in synaptic vesicles called **SV2A** and reduces transmitter release. It works for many seizure types, has almost no drug interactions and can be given by IV. The main side effects are irritability, mood changes and sleepiness.

**Topiramate** works in several ways and also blocks the enzyme **carbonic anhydrase**. This can cause kidney stones, tingling, weight loss and slowed thinking or word-finding problems. It is also used to prevent migraines.

**Lamotrigine** is broad too, although it can worsen myoclonic jerks in some people.

**Newer drugs** include **perampanel** (blocks AMPA glutamate receptors), **cenobamate** (very effective for difficult focal epilepsy) and **brivaracetam** (a stronger SV2A drug). Some medicines target rare childhood epilepsies, like **stiripentol** and **fenfluramine** for Dravet syndrome and **rufinamide** for Lennox–Gastaut syndrome.
levels.college:
**Valproate**
- Mechanisms: Na+ channel blockade, T-type Ca2+ reduction, increased GABA (GABA-T and succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase inhibition), and histone deacetylase inhibition.
- Spectrum: focal, generalized tonic-clonic, absence, myoclonic; also bipolar mania and migraine prevention.
- Toxicity: hepatotoxicity (highest in children under 2 on polytherapy and with **POLG** mutations, where it is contraindicated), pancreatitis, thrombocytopenia, **hyperammonemic encephalopathy** (carnitine may help), weight gain, tremor, alopecia, polycystic ovary features.
- Teratogenicity: neural tube defects, cardiac and facial malformations, dose-related reduction in child IQ and increased autism risk. Regulators require pregnancy prevention programs.
- Interactions: **CYP and UGT inhibitor** (raises lamotrigine, phenobarbital); highly protein-bound and displaces phenytoin.

**Levetiracetam/brivaracetam:** bind **SV2A**, a synaptic vesicle glycoprotein, reducing vesicle release under high-frequency activity. Renally cleared, minimal interactions, IV formulation. Behavioral effects (irritability, depression, rarely psychosis); pyridoxine is sometimes tried for irritability, with limited evidence. Brivaracetam has roughly 15–30-fold higher SV2A affinity and faster brain entry.

**Topiramate:** Na+ block, GABA-A potentiation, AMPA/kainate antagonism, **carbonic anhydrase inhibition** → normal anion gap metabolic acidosis, calcium phosphate stones, paresthesias, oligohidrosis/hyperthermia in children, acute angle-closure glaucoma, cognitive slowing, weight loss, teratogenicity (oral clefts). **Zonisamide** shares several features (sulfonamide, stones).

**Newer agents:**
- **Perampanel**: noncompetitive AMPA antagonist; boxed warning for psychiatric and behavioral reactions (aggression, hostility).
- **Cenobamate**: reduces persistent Na+ current and positively modulates GABA-A; high seizure-freedom rates in trials; DRESS with fast titration, so slow titration is required; shortens QT (contraindicated in familial short QT).
- **Felbamate**: NMDA (NR2B) antagonist; aplastic anemia and hepatic failure restrict it to refractory cases.
- Syndrome-specific: **rufinamide** (LGS; QT shortening), **stiripentol** (Dravet; GABA-A modulator and CYP inhibitor), **fenfluramine** (Dravet, LGS; serotonergic, echocardiographic monitoring for valve disease), **everolimus** (TSC; mTOR inhibitor), **ganaxolone** (CDKL5).
levels.phd:
**SV2A: an unexpected target.** Levetiracetam was discovered by in vivo screening in audiogenic and kindled rodent models, not by target-based design, and only later was SV2A identified by photoaffinity labeling. SV2A-knockout mice have severe seizures; heterozygotes show reduced levetiracetam efficacy, and binding affinity across analogues correlates with anticonvulsant potency. SV2A may regulate synaptotagmin trafficking and vesicle priming, so the drug likely acts as a use-dependent brake on release, explaining its broad spectrum. Brivaracetam's higher affinity and padsevonil (SV2A/B/C plus benzodiazepine-site partial agonism, failed phase 2b/3) show the limits of simply increasing SV2A binding.

**Valproate's teratogenicity** has a plausible epigenetic basis: HDAC inhibition alters expression of genes in neural tube closure and neurodevelopment. The dose-dependent IQ reduction (NEAD study) and autism signal (Danish registry) shaped European restrictions, now extended to paternal exposure caution in some jurisdictions after observational signals of neurodevelopmental risk in children of fathers treated around conception, though causality remains uncertain.

**Cenobamate's efficacy** (in the pivotal trial, about a fifth of patients on the highest arm were seizure-free during maintenance, extraordinary for refractory focal epilepsy) may reflect dual Na+ persistent-current inhibition and GABA-A modulation at a non-benzodiazepine site. DRESS seen with rapid titration disappeared in a slow-titration safety study, an instance of titration rate as a determinant of immune toxicity.

**Fenfluramine** acts on serotonin release and 5-HT1D, 5-HT2C and σ1 receptors; in Dravet syndrome it reduced convulsive seizure frequency substantially. Valvulopathy (5-HT2B agonism by norfenfluramine), which ended its earlier use for weight loss, has not been seen in the monitored epilepsy programs.

**Precision therapy:** everolimus in TSC addresses the mTOR pathway itself; antisense oligonucleotides (zorevunersen) upregulating productive SCN1A transcripts and gene therapy for Dravet syndrome aim at disease modification rather than seizure suppression, a conceptual shift from symptomatic ASMs.
levels.expert:
**Valproate: the hardest conversation in epilepsy.** It is the most effective drug for many idiopathic generalized epilepsies, especially juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, yet it carries the highest teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risk. For anyone who could become pregnant, choose levetiracetam or lamotrigine first; if valproate is truly needed, document informed consent and pregnancy prevention, and review at least yearly. Never stop it abruptly in an established pregnancy without specialist input; seizures carry risks too.

**Safety checks for valproate:** liver tests and platelets at baseline and early; rule out POLG disease (Alpers) in children with unexplained developmental regression or liver disease before using it; measure ammonia in a confused patient even with normal liver tests.

**Levetiracetam:** a workhorse in hospital because it is IV, interaction-free and easy to start. Ask about mood and irritability at every visit; in a teenager with depression or anger on levetiracetam, switching often helps.

**Topiramate:** warn about word-finding difficulty and slowed thinking; advise fluids for stones; acute eye pain with blurred vision means urgent assessment for angle-closure glaucoma. It reduces the effect of estrogen contraceptives at higher exposures and is teratogenic.

**Cenobamate:** consider early in drug-resistant focal epilepsy; titrate slowly to avoid DRESS; it raises phenytoin and phenobarbital and lowers lamotrigine and carbamazepine levels, so adjust co-medications.

**Perampanel:** screen for psychiatric history and warn families about aggression.

**Syndromes need syndrome drugs:** Dravet (valproate, clobazam, stiripentol, fenfluramine; avoid Na+ blockers), Lennox–Gastaut (valproate, lamotrigine, rufinamide, clobazam, fenfluramine), TSC (vigabatrin, everolimus). Early epilepsy-center referral and genetic testing in children with refractory epilepsy pay off, because a diagnosis can directly change the drug.

keyPoints: Valproate: broad-spectrum (Na+, T-type Ca2+, GABA); hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, hyperammonemia; highest teratogenic risk.
Levetiracetam/brivaracetam bind SV2A; renal, few interactions; irritability and mood effects.
Topiramate inhibits carbonic anhydrase: kidney stones, acidosis, cognitive slowing, angle-closure glaucoma.
Perampanel blocks AMPA receptors (psychiatric warning); cenobamate needs slow titration (DRESS).
Syndrome-specific drugs: stiripentol and fenfluramine (Dravet), rufinamide (LGS), everolimus and vigabatrin (TSC).

lessons.title: Status Epilepticus

levels.kid:
Most seizures stop by themselves in a minute or two. But sometimes a seizure keeps going, or seizures come one after another without the person waking up in between. This is called **status epilepticus**, and it is an emergency.

The longer it lasts, the harder it is to stop, and the brain can get hurt. So doctors act fast, like firefighters putting out a fire before it spreads.

First they make sure the person can breathe. Then they give a fast calming medicine. If that doesn't work, they give a second medicine. If it still doesn't stop, the person goes to intensive care for very strong sleep medicines while doctors watch the brain waves.
levels.hs:
**Status epilepticus** is a seizure that lasts too long or repeated seizures without recovery in between. Doctors treat any convulsive seizure lasting **5 minutes or more** as status epilepticus, because seizures that pass this point rarely stop on their own. After about 30 minutes, the risk of lasting brain injury rises.

**Why time matters:** during a long seizure, the brain pulls GABA-A receptors (brakes) inside the cell and adds more NMDA glutamate receptors (gas). So benzodiazepines work worse the longer you wait.

**The treatment steps:**
1. **Stabilize:** airway, breathing, circulation, oxygen, check blood sugar, IV access. Give glucose if low and thiamine when malnutrition or alcohol use disorder is possible.
2. **First line (0–5 minutes in):** a **benzodiazepine**: IV lorazepam, or IM, nasal or buccal midazolam if there is no IV, or IV diazepam.
3. **Second line:** if seizures continue, **levetiracetam**, **fosphenytoin** or **valproate** IV. A large trial (ESETT) found these work about equally well.
4. **Refractory status:** if seizures still continue, intensive care with intubation and anesthetic infusions such as **midazolam**, **propofol** or **pentobarbital**, guided by continuous EEG.

Doctors also search for the cause: low sodium or sugar, infection, stroke, stopping seizure medicine or poisoning.
levels.college:
**Definitions (ILAE 2015).** Two time points: **t1**, when a seizure is unlikely to stop spontaneously and treatment should begin (5 minutes for tonic-clonic status), and **t2**, after which long-term consequences become likely (30 minutes for tonic-clonic). Focal status with impaired awareness has t1 about 10 minutes and t2 over 60 minutes. Refractory SE persists despite a benzodiazepine and one second-line drug; super-refractory SE continues 24 hours or more after anesthesia is started or recurs on weaning.

**Pharmacoresistance develops quickly.** Prolonged seizures trigger clathrin-mediated **endocytosis of synaptic GABA-A receptors** (β2/3 and γ2 subunits) and trafficking of **NMDA receptors** to the synapse. Benzodiazepine potency can fall dramatically within 30 minutes in animal models, while NMDA-mediated excitotoxicity rises.

**Evidence base:**
- **RAMPART:** prehospital IM midazolam was at least as effective as IV lorazepam (faster to give).
- **ESETT:** in benzodiazepine-refractory SE, levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate each stopped seizures in roughly half of patients, with similar safety; ConSEPT and EcLiPSE in children were consistent.
- Under-treatment with inadequate benzodiazepine is common and associated with worse outcomes.

**Second-line agent choice:** fosphenytoin (hypotension, arrhythmia; avoid in toxin-induced seizures, which it may worsen), valproate (avoid in liver disease, mitochondrial disease, pregnancy when alternatives exist), levetiracetam (renal adjustment, few interactions). **Phenobarbital** is an alternative.

**Refractory SE:** continuous midazolam, propofol (propofol infusion syndrome: acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, cardiac failure) or pentobarbital/thiopental (hypotension, ileus, immunosuppression), titrated to seizure suppression or burst suppression on continuous EEG.

**Cause-specific therapy:** hypoglycemia (dextrose), Wernicke risk (thiamine), hyponatremia (hypertonic saline), eclampsia (**magnesium sulfate**), isoniazid toxicity (**pyridoxine**), autoimmune encephalitis (immunotherapy).
levels.phd:
**Receptor trafficking as the core pathophysiology.** In lithium–pilocarpine and kainate models, synaptic GABA-A receptors containing γ2 are internalized via dephosphorylation of β3 S408/S409 and AP2 binding, while extrasynaptic δ-containing receptors (benzodiazepine-insensitive) are relatively spared. Simultaneously, NR1/NR2B NMDA receptors move to synaptic membranes through PKC- and Src-dependent mechanisms. This dual shift underlies the time-dependent loss of benzodiazepine efficacy and the rationale for early polytherapy: combining a benzodiazepine with an NMDA antagonist and a second agent was more effective than escalating monotherapy in rodent models (Wasterlain and colleagues).

**Neuronal injury.** Excitotoxic Ca2+ overload, mitochondrial failure, reactive oxygen species and inflammatory signaling (IL-1β, HMGB1) cause neuronal loss even with peripheral paralysis and controlled systemic physiology, showing that seizure activity itself injures neurons (Meldrum's paralyzed baboon experiments). Biomarkers such as neuron-specific enolase rise after prolonged SE.

**Nonconvulsive SE (NCSE)** is common in comatose ICU patients; continuous EEG detects electrographic seizures in a substantial minority. The Salzburg criteria define EEG diagnosis. Whether aggressive anesthetic suppression of NCSE improves outcome is unresolved, and anesthetic infusions carry independent risks; a measured approach balances harms.

**New-onset refractory status epilepticus (NORSE)** and its febrile subtype (FIRES) are often autoimmune or cryptogenic; cytokine-directed therapies (anakinra blocking IL-1, tocilizumab blocking IL-6) and ketogenic diet have emerging evidence, an example of mechanism-based therapy in SE.

**Pharmacokinetics in critical illness:** hypoalbuminemia raises free phenytoin and valproate; augmented renal clearance lowers levetiracetam; carbapenems markedly reduce valproate levels via inhibition of valproyl-glucuronide hydrolysis, a classic interaction that can precipitate breakthrough SE.
levels.expert:
**Run it like a resuscitation, with a clock.** Note the time of onset. At 5 minutes, give a full benzodiazepine dose promptly; the most common error worldwide is giving too little, too late, and repeating it too timidly. If no IV, IM or intranasal midazolam is as good. Repeat once if needed, then move to second line by about 20 minutes without waiting.

**Second line:** choose by patient. Levetiracetam in liver disease or many interactions; valproate in known generalized epilepsy (avoid in pregnancy, liver disease, mitochondrial disease); fosphenytoin when cardiac monitoring is available and no toxin is suspected. If one fails, many clinicians try another rapidly before intubation, but refractory SE should not wait long for anesthesia.

**Find and fix the cause in parallel:** glucose at the bedside, sodium, calcium, magnesium, drug levels in known epilepsy (missed doses are the commonest cause in people with epilepsy), toxicology, CT head, and lumbar puncture if infection is possible (start antimicrobials and acyclovir empirically). In late pregnancy or postpartum, think eclampsia and give magnesium sulfate. In a suspected isoniazid overdose, give pyridoxine, because benzodiazepines will not work without it.

**After convulsions stop:** if the patient does not wake up within the expected time, get an EEG to exclude nonconvulsive status. Many "post-ictal" patients are still seizing.

**Refractory SE in the ICU:** intubate, start a midazolam or propofol infusion, connect continuous EEG, and set a clear target (seizure suppression or burst suppression) for a defined period before a slow wean while maintenance ASMs are optimized. Watch for propofol infusion syndrome with prolonged use (rising lactate, CK, triglycerides).

**Neurosurgical links:** status can be the first sign of a tumor, abscess or bleed, and lesional super-refractory SE occasionally leads to emergency resective surgery. Early neurosurgical input matters when imaging shows a structural cause.

keyPoints: Convulsive seizure lasting 5 minutes or more = status epilepticus; injury risk rises after about 30 minutes.
Prolonged seizures internalize GABA-A and add synaptic NMDA receptors, so benzodiazepines lose potency over time.
First line: a benzodiazepine (IV lorazepam, IM/intranasal midazolam, IV diazepam), given fast and in adequate amount.
Second line: levetiracetam, fosphenytoin or valproate (similar efficacy in ESETT).
Refractory: ICU anesthetic infusions (midazolam, propofol, pentobarbital) with continuous EEG.
Treat causes: glucose, thiamine, sodium, magnesium for eclampsia, pyridoxine for isoniazid.

kidTest.q: A seizure that keeps going and won't stop is:
kidTest.explain: Status epilepticus is an emergency.

kidTest.q: Doctors act fast, like:
kidTest.explain: Speed matters, like stopping a fire before it spreads.

kidTest.q: The very first thing doctors check is that the person can:
kidTest.explain: Breathing comes first.

kidTest.q: The longer a seizure lasts, the ___ it is to stop.
kidTest.explain: Long seizures get harder to stop.

kidTest.q: If the first medicine doesn't work, doctors:
kidTest.explain: They move to a second medicine quickly.

advancedTest.q: A patient on valproate for epilepsy is started on meropenem and develops breakthrough status. The mechanism is:
choices: Carbapenems inhibit hydrolysis of valproyl-glucuronide, sharply lowering valproate levels
advancedTest.explain: The interaction is large and not overcome by raising valproate; switch agents.

advancedTest.q: Experimental support for combination therapy early in status comes from the fact that prolonged seizures:
choices: Reduce synaptic GABA-A while increasing synaptic NMDA receptors
advancedTest.explain: Targeting both the weakened inhibitory and strengthened excitatory side was more effective in models.

advancedTest.q: Why is fosphenytoin avoided in seizures caused by many drug overdoses?
choices: It is ineffective and may worsen some toxin-induced seizures and cardiotoxicity
advancedTest.explain: Toxin-induced seizures respond to GABAergic drugs; phenytoin can add Na+ channel cardiotoxicity.

advancedTest.q: Meldrum's paralyzed, ventilated primate experiments showed that:
choices: Systemic hypoxia alone causes seizure brain injury
Seizure activity itself causes neuronal injury even with controlled systemic physiology
advancedTest.explain: Neuronal loss occurred despite paralysis and ventilation, implicating excitotoxicity.
